name: A typical “journey of a young architect” plots architecture complexity against the developer's experience. Which statements describe this journey?

answers.body: At first architecture visibly helps, so the complexity of the architectures the developer builds grows.
The curve reaches a peak of over-engineered, excessive architecture, which is a necessary waypoint towards pragmatic architecture.
After the peak, complexity drops and settles at “architectural enlightenment”: picking the correct amount of architecture the project needs.
Experienced architects always choose the most complex architecture available.
answers.comment: L6, slides 9-10: Experience leads to choosing the amount of architecture the project needs.

name: Consider the complexity of the architecture versus the complexity of the problem we are trying to solve. Which combinations are a good fit?

answers.body: Simple app + simple architecture
Complex app + complex architecture
Simple app + complex architecture
answers.comment: L6, slide 16: a mismatch – unnecessary complexity.

answers.body: Complex app + simple architecture
answers.comment: L6, slide 17: a mismatch – the architecture cannot cope with the problem.

answers.body: Any combination, because architecture is a single one-dimensional choice that does not depend on the problem.
answers.comment: L6, slides 19-20: Architecture is not one-dimensional; it is a mosaic of complementary decisions.

name: Architecture as a code structure decides how code is divided into blocks. Which observations indicate that a codebase needs MORE structure?

answers.body: Frequent merge conflicts in “god” services or files.
Framework/ORM choices leak everywhere and the team feels locked in.
Onboarding is slow because the code layout does not match how the business thinks.
Many layers, DTOs and mappers exist even for trivial CRUD.
answers.comment: L6, slide 22: ceremony overload – a sign of too much structure.

answers.body: Simple features require touching 6+ layers or 10+ files.
answers.comment: L6, slide 22: a sign of too much structure.

name: Architecture decisions were presented along three dimensions: code structure, deployment and problem modeling. Which statements about their goals are correct?

answers.body: Code structure and deployment both aim to maximize cohesion, minimize coupling, define modules/components around business capabilities and support future proofing and replaceability – deployment just on a bigger scale.
Problem modeling aims to capture business meaning, force the system to follow business rules, prevent developers from making mistakes and improve testability.
In clean architecture your job is not to solve how data flow and are stored in a system, but to solve business problems with code.
Each architectural style differs only in its complexity, so choosing an architecture means choosing a point on one axis.
answers.comment: L6, slides 20-21, 35: Architecture is a mosaic of decisions and each style has many dimensions, not just complexity.

answers.body: The goal of code structure is to maximize coupling so that every module can call every other module directly.
answers.comment: L6, slides 21, 41: Minimize coupling; everyone knowing everyone is a sign of bad design.

name: Which statements compare three-layer architecture with clean architecture correctly?

answers.body: Three-layer architecture clearly separates UI, business and data logic and is super easy for CRUD-heavy applications.
Three-layer architecture intuitively leads towards data-driven design.
Clean architecture focuses on solving business problems (use cases) and tends to ignore how data will finally be persisted.
In clean architecture, business logic is stored in use cases, which request needed dependencies (ports) without caring about their implementation (adapters).
Clean architecture puts the repository implementation into the domain, next to the use cases.
answers.comment: L6, slide 27: The domain holds use cases, entities and repository interfaces; the repository implementation belongs to the data side.

name: A clean-architecture use case AddTransactionUseCase(userId, amount, description, expiration) is handled by a handler that declares a transaction repository, a current-user provider and a mediator as dependencies; it loads the balance through a specification, throws an exception for a negative balance, creates the transaction, publishes a UserBalanceChanged notification and finally saves the transaction. What does this illustrate?

answers.body: The request record contains only the part the UI needs.
The handler just requests data without caring how it is retrieved.
The main focus is on the business rule; dependent actions are triggered by publishing a notification instead of being performed in the handler.
Saving data is kind of an afterthought.
The handler should open the database connection and build the SQL itself, so that the business rule knows how data is stored.
answers.comment: L6, slides 26, 31: Ignoring persistence helps design better solutions.

name: Architecture as a deployment choice decides how code is divided into executables. Which observations indicate that you need MORE separate applications (services)?

answers.body: Many teams work side by side.
Releases are slow or risky because one big deploy blocks everyone.
Different parts need different scalability.
There are too many services for the team size and everyone touches everything.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: a sign that you need fewer separate apps.

answers.body: You always deploy everything together anyway.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: a sign that you need fewer separate apps.

name: Which statements about the modular monolith are correct?

answers.body: The system is designed as if it were a microservice architecture, but the step of hosting each service separately (and its communication pain) is skipped.
Each service is a separate module/project, and implementation is kept separate from communication definitions: the messages (requests, notifications) are shared, the implementation stays hidden.
Code spread across many loosely coupled projects helps when the monolith needs to be split.
A sign of good design is that every module knows every other module (“small village”).
answers.comment: L6, slide 41: Everyone knowing everyone is the small village syndrome – an indicator of bad design.

answers.body: It is a recommended starting point for most projects whose future is unknown, together with clean architecture.

name: When and how should a module of a modular monolith be turned into a separate application (a “satellite”)?

answers.body: When the module has become large and self-sufficient.
When a large portion of traffic flows through it and more instances would help, or a team now mainly handles it.
Steps: define boundaries, move it to a separate app, and redirect the right messages from in-process to cross-app communication.
The first satellite is hard: authentication, messaging (protocol choice, asynchronous execution) and data storage must be solved.
Immediately at project start, every module should be launched as a satellite.
answers.comment: L6, slides 37-38: Start simple and upgrade on pain; most projects do not need microservices.

name: Architecture as a problem-modeling choice shapes how the business is modeled. Which observations indicate that you need MORE sophisticated domain modeling?

answers.body: Invariants keep breaking and the same bug resurfaces in different places.
Schema-driven thinking: features are described as tables/DTOs, not domain concepts.
Teams use different terms for the same concept (no shared language).
Heavy DDD is used for simple CRUD, with aggregates that just wrap a few fields.
answers.comment: L6, slide 47: a sign that the modeling is too complex.

answers.body: Stakeholders cannot follow the diagrams because the language drifted from the business.
answers.comment: L6, slide 47: a sign that the modeling is too complex.

name: Which statements about Domain Driven Design (DDD) are correct?

answers.body: The main concept is that a domain object (aggregate root) is always valid.
No public setters on properties and no mutable lists are exposed; e.g. a collection is exposed as IReadOnlyCollection while the list itself is private.
All changes must come through public methods on the aggregate root, even when they change an inner entity.
Cross-domain communication is done only via domain events.
Inner entities of an aggregate may be modified directly by any other aggregate.
answers.comment: L6, slides 56-57: Changes go through the aggregate root; other domains communicate by events.

name: Which DDD terms are matched with a correct description?

answers.body: Bounded context – a boundary within which a model and its language apply; the same concept (e.g. Customer or Product) can appear in both a sales and a support context.
answers.comment: L6, slide 49 shows a Sales Context and a Support Context that both contain Customer and Product; the one-line definition is general DDD wording, not slide text.

answers.body: Aggregate root – the entity that represents the aggregate and through which its aggregate boundary is accessed.
Domain event – something that happened in the domain (e.g. OrderStarted) and is handled by one or more event handlers.
Inner entity – an entity that other aggregates reference and modify directly.
answers.comment: L6, slides 51, 56: Inner entities are changed only through the aggregate root.

name: Which recommendations summarize pragmatic architecture (“start simple, upgrade on pain”)?

answers.body: It is OK to skip architecture or start with something simple for prototypes and hobby projects.
Starting complex (e.g. DDD microservices) is a good idea for high traffic, complex business and many teams.
When you do not know whether the project ends in a year or survives ten, start with something a little bit overkill with clear upgrade paths, e.g. clean architecture and a modular monolith.
Increase complexity slowly as the project grows (add DDD if the business is complex, spin up satellites when needed) and do not be afraid to make the jump a little too early.
About 90 % of software projects need a microservice architecture from day one.
answers.comment: L6, slide 37: The opposite – 90 % of projects do not need microservices.

name: Open question: a startup with three developers builds an internal booking system. Today it is mostly CRUD with a few business rules, but nobody knows whether the product will be dropped within a year or grow for ten years with more teams and traffic. Recommend an architecture along the three dimensions – code structure, deployment and problem modeling – and justify it. For each dimension name the signals that would tell you to add more (or less) architecture later.
answer: Architecture is a mosaic of complementary decisions, not one choice; the aim is to fit its complexity to the problem's complexity. Because the future is unknown, follow “start simple, upgrade on pain”: start with something a little bit overkill that has clear upgrade paths. Code structure: clean architecture – business logic in use cases that request dependencies through ports, implementations in adapters, persistence treated as an afterthought; this keeps cohesion high, coupling low and modules aligned with business capabilities. Add structure when merge conflicts concentrate in “god” files, framework/ORM choices leak everywhere or onboarding is slow because the layout does not match the business; reduce it when trivial CRUD needs many layers/DTOs/mappers, tests are mostly mocks/wiring or simple features touch 6+ layers or 10+ files. Deployment: a modular monolith – modules designed as if they were services (separate projects, shared message contracts, hidden implementations) but deployed together; no microservices yet (90 % of projects do not need them). Launch a satellite when a module becomes large and self-sufficient, carries much traffic needing more instances, or gets its own team; signals for more separate apps are many teams side by side, slow/risky big deploys and different scalability needs; signals for fewer are too many services for the team size or always deploying everything. Expect the first satellite to require solving authentication, messaging and data storage. Problem modeling: use-case-oriented modeling first; add DDD (aggregate roots that are always valid, no public setters, changes only through the root, cross-domain events, bounded contexts) when invariants keep breaking, features are described as tables/DTOs or teams use different terms for the same concept; avoid it while it would only wrap CRUD fields or drift from the business language.
keyPoints: Architecture = several complementary dimensions; fit complexity to the problem
Unknown future: start a little overkill with upgrade paths (start simple, upgrade on pain)
Deployment: modular monolith; satellite indicators; more/fewer-apps indicators
Modeling: add DDD when invariants break / no shared language; avoid heavy DDD for CRUD
Microservices not needed for most projects at the start
source: L6, slides 13-22, 27, 35-47, 53-57, 64-71; the step “use-case-oriented modeling first” is inferred from the complexity axis facades → use cases → DDD (slide 47) and slide 70
